stem: An interviewer asks you to define the Model Context Protocol in one sentence. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: An agent framework that plans multi-step tasks and decides which tool the model should call next
options.why: Planning and tool choice belong to the host and its model. MCP only defines how tools and context are discovered and invoked.

options.text: A fine-tuning technique that teaches a model to emit JSON function calls
options.why: MCP does not change model weights. It is a client-server protocol built on JSON-RPC 2.0.

options.text: An open standard for connecting AI applications to external tools and data
options.why: That is the official framing: MCP is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems.

options.text: A hosted vector database that stores conversation context for large language models
options.why: MCP stores nothing; it is a wire protocol. A vector store could sit behind an MCP server, but it is not MCP.

explanation: MCP is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications (hosts such as Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code or Cursor) to external systems through servers that expose tools, resources and prompts. It is not a model, a database or an agent framework. Interviewers use this opener to check that you can separate the protocol from the things built around it.

stem: Your company has 4 AI applications and wants each of them to use the same 6 internal tools. Without a shared protocol every app needs a custom connector to every tool. If every app instead speaks MCP as a client and every tool is wrapped once as an MCP server, how many integrations (clients plus servers) must be built in total? Type a number.
explanation: Point-to-point integration needs N x M = 4 x 6 = 24 connectors. With a shared protocol each app implements the client side once and each tool implements the server side once, so the work becomes N + M = 4 + 6 = 10. This N x M to N + M reduction is the standard answer to "why does MCP exist?".

stem: Match each MCP architecture term with the description that fits it.

options.text: MCP client
options.why: A connector instance bound to a single server.

options.text: Transport layer
options.why: Framing, connection setup and authorization.

options.text: MCP server
options.why: A program that serves tools, resources and prompts.

options.text: MCP host
options.why: The AI application that owns the model and the user.

prompts.text: The AI application that creates connections, owns the model and enforces user consent
A component that keeps a dedicated connection to exactly one server
A program that exposes tools, resources and prompts, locally or remotely
The part of MCP that handles message framing, connection setup and HTTP authorization

explanation: The host (for example VS Code or Claude Desktop) creates one MCP client per server it connects to; each client has a 1:1 relationship with its server. Servers provide context and capabilities. MCP itself has two layers: the data layer (JSON-RPC messages, discovery, primitives) and the transport layer (stdio or Streamable HTTP framing, connection handling and authorization).

stem: MCP only works with Claude-based applications, because Anthropic created the protocol.

options.text: True
options.why: The protocol is vendor-neutral; nothing in it is tied to one model provider.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. MCP is an open standard supported by many hosts, including ChatGPT, Visual Studio Code and Cursor.

explanation: Anthropic introduced MCP, but it is an open protocol with an open, community-driven specification process. The official introduction lists Claude, ChatGPT, Visual Studio Code, Cursor and others as hosts. A server written once can be used from any compliant host, which is the whole point of the standard.

stem: Which three primitives can an MCP server expose to clients?

options.text: Agents, memories and workflows
options.why: These are agent-framework concepts. MCP does not define agents or memories as primitives.

options.text: Resources, roots and notifications
options.why: Roots is a (now deprecated) client feature and notifications are a message type, not a primitive.

options.text: Tools, sampling and elicitation
options.why: Sampling and elicitation are client features that servers ask the client for; they are not exposed by servers.

options.text: Tools, resources and prompts
options.why: These are the three core server primitives defined by the data layer.

explanation: Servers expose tools (executable functions the model can invoke), resources (data that provides context) and prompts (reusable interaction templates). Each has `*/list` methods for discovery, plus `tools/call`, `resources/read` and `prompts/get` for use. Client-side features such as elicitation are a separate category.

stem: Which of these JSON messages is a JSON-RPC **notification**?

options.text: `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "tools/list", "params": {}}`
options.why: A `method` plus an `id` makes this a request, which expects a response.

options.text: `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "result": {"resultType": "complete", "tools": []}}`
options.why: An `id` with a `result` is a successful response to request 7.

options.text: `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/progress", "params": {"progressToken": "t1", "progress": 3}}`
options.why: It has a `method` and no `id`, so it is a one-way message and the receiver must not reply.

options.text: `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "error": {"code": -32601, "message": "Method not found"}}`
options.why: An `id` with an `error` object is an error response to request 7.

explanation: JSON-RPC distinguishes messages by shape: requests have `method` and `id`; responses have `id` plus either `result` or `error`; notifications have `method` but **must not** include an `id`, and the receiver must not send a response. Progress, cancellation and list-changed messages are all notifications.

stem: A teammate says: "The GitHub MCP server is remote because it exposes tools, while the filesystem server is local because it exposes resources." What is the correct distinction?

options.text: Local servers may only expose resources, while remote servers may only expose tools
options.why: Nothing restricts primitives by location. A local server can expose tools and a remote one can expose resources.

options.text: Remote servers must be written in TypeScript and local servers in Python
options.why: Language is irrelevant; every official SDK supports both transports.

options.text: It depends on where the server runs and its transport: a stdio subprocess versus a hosted HTTP service
options.why: Correct. The same primitives can be served either way; location and transport define local versus remote.

options.text: A server counts as remote whenever it calls an external API over the internet, even if the host launches it as a local subprocess
options.why: A subprocess launched over stdio is a local server even if it calls the internet internally.

explanation: "MCP server" means the program that serves context, wherever it runs. A server launched by the host as a child process over stdio is commonly called local; one running as a service reached over Streamable HTTP (for example Sentry's hosted server) is called remote. Local stdio servers typically serve one client, while remote servers typically serve many.

stem: Your service already has a well-documented REST API. What is the main thing an MCP server adds on top of it for AI applications?

options.text: It replaces the need for authentication, because hosts are trusted
options.why: Remote MCP servers still need authentication; the spec defines an OAuth 2.1-based framework for HTTP.

options.text: Lower latency, because MCP messages are binary-encoded instead of JSON
options.why: MCP messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 encoded as UTF-8 JSON; there is no binary speed advantage.

options.text: Any MCP host can discover and call its self-describing capabilities at runtime, with no app-specific glue
options.why: This is the core value: runtime discovery plus a uniform invocation contract that every host understands.

options.text: REST endpoints cannot be described to language models at all, so wrapping them in MCP is the only way an AI app can call them
options.why: Hosts can wrap REST calls as custom function-calling tools. MCP standardises that wrapping so it is reusable across hosts.

explanation: A REST API is designed for application developers, and each AI app would need hand-written glue to describe and call it. An MCP server exposes capabilities in a form any MCP host can list (`tools/list`), understand (names, descriptions, JSON Schemas) and invoke (`tools/call`). Often the MCP server simply wraps the existing REST API.

stem: A host application is connected to a local filesystem server, a local database server and a remote Sentry server. How many MCP clients does the host run, and why?

options.text: Zero, because the model talks to the servers directly
options.why: The model never connects to servers; the host's clients do, and the host passes results to the model.

options.text: One, because a single client can multiplex all servers over one connection
options.why: MCP clients are not multiplexers. Each client communicates with exactly one server.

options.text: Three: each client holds a dedicated connection to exactly one server
options.why: The host creates one client per server; the 1:1 relationship keeps security boundaries between servers.

options.text: Two, one per transport type, because the two stdio servers can share a client
options.why: Clients are per server, not per transport. Two stdio servers mean two subprocesses and two clients.

explanation: In MCP, a host creates and manages multiple clients, and each client has a 1:1 relationship with a particular server. This gives each server its own connection and keeps security boundaries: one server cannot see another server's traffic. The host may even run two clients against the same remote server.

stem: Where does the language model sit in the MCP architecture? (Choose two.)

options.text: The host owns the model and the full conversation; servers receive only the requests the client sends them
options.why: This matches the design principle that the full conversation history stays with the host.

options.text: Servers can read other servers' tool results to coordinate work
options.why: Servers must not "see into" other servers. Cross-server interaction is controlled by the host.

options.text: The model opens its own connection to each server and calls tools directly
options.why: The model only emits tool-use requests. The host's MCP client performs the actual `tools/call`.

options.text: A server never sees the conversation unless the host deliberately includes parts of it in a request
options.why: Servers should not be able to read the whole conversation; they get only the context they need.

options.text: Each MCP server embeds its own model, which the host queries through `tools/call`
options.why: Servers do not need a model at all; most simply run code or fetch data.

explanation: One of MCP's design principles is that servers should not be able to read the whole conversation, nor see into other servers. The host coordinates the model, aggregates context and decides what to send to each server. A server only sees the requests addressed to it.

stem: Put the steps of a typical tool invocation in order, from discovery to the result reaching the model.

options.text: The host adds the tool result to the conversation so the model can continue
The server executes the tool and returns a result with `content`
The model decides to use a tool and emits a tool-use request with arguments
The client sends `tools/list` and receives the server's tool definitions
The host adds those tool definitions to the model's available tools
The host's client sends `tools/call` with the tool name and arguments to the right server

explanation: Discovery comes first (`tools/list`), then the host exposes the tools to the model. The model chooses a tool, but it is the host's MCP client that routes the `tools/call` to the server owning that tool. The result goes back to the host, which inserts it into the model's context. Interviewers look for the point that the model never talks to the server directly.

stem: "If the model already supports function calling, why do we need MCP?" Which answer is most accurate?

options.text: They are complementary: the model picks tools via function calling, and MCP is how the host discovers and runs them
options.why: Right: the model still uses function calling, and MCP supplies the tools it can call.

options.text: MCP replaces function calling: once a host speaks MCP, the model no longer emits tool calls and the server decides which tool to run
options.why: Models do not speak MCP. The host translates MCP tool definitions into the model's function-calling format.

options.text: Function calling only works for local code, while MCP only works for remote APIs
options.why: Neither is limited that way; MCP servers can be local (stdio) or remote (HTTP).

options.text: They are the same thing under different vendor names
options.why: They operate at different layers: one is a model capability, the other a client-server protocol.

explanation: Function or tool calling is a model capability: given tool schemas, the model emits a structured call. MCP sits around it: the host lists tools from MCP servers, passes their schemas to the model, and when the model emits a call, the host's MCP client executes it with `tools/call`. MCP makes tools portable across hosts and models.

stem: MCP is described as two layers: a data layer and a transport layer. Which of these belong to the **data layer**? (Choose two.)

options.text: The `tools/list` and `tools/call` methods and their result shapes
options.why: Primitives and their methods are defined by the JSON-RPC data layer.

options.text: Version and capability discovery through `server/discover`
options.why: Discovery of versions and capabilities is part of the data layer.

options.text: Choosing between a single JSON body and an SSE stream for a reply
options.why: That is a Streamable HTTP transport decision.

options.text: Newline-delimited framing of messages over stdin and stdout
options.why: Message framing is a transport concern (the stdio binding).

options.text: Sending a bearer token in the HTTP `Authorization` header
options.why: Authorization for HTTP is handled by the transport layer.

explanation: The data layer defines the JSON-RPC protocol: discovery, server features (tools, resources, prompts), client features and utilities such as notifications and progress. The transport layer defines channels: connection setup, framing (stdio lines or HTTP POST/SSE) and authorization. The same data-layer messages work unchanged on every transport.

stem: A product manager asks whether adopting MCP means you can retire your RAG pipeline. What is the best answer?

options.text: No. RAG is a retrieval technique; MCP is a protocol that can expose your retriever as a tool
options.why: They solve different problems and compose well: MCP can be the way a host reaches your retriever.

options.text: Yes. MCP servers automatically index your documents and inject the most relevant chunks into the prompt
options.why: MCP does no indexing or ranking; a server must implement retrieval itself if it wants to offer it.

options.text: No, because MCP cannot carry text content back to the model
options.why: Tool results and resources commonly carry text content.

options.text: Yes, because MCP resources are always loaded into the model's context in full
options.why: How resources are used is up to the host; nothing forces full loading, and large corpora still need retrieval.

explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation decides *what* context to fetch (embedding, search, ranking). MCP standardises *how* an AI application reaches a capability. A common design is an MCP server that wraps the vector search as a `search_docs` tool, or exposes documents as resources, so any host can use the same RAG backend.

stem: Which of these 2026-07-28 client requests is **invalid** under MCP's JSON-RPC rules?

options.text: `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": null, "method": "tools/list", "params": {...}}`
options.why: MCP requires a string or integer ID and explicitly forbids `null`, even though base JSON-RPC allows it.

options.text: `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": "req-9f2", "method": "tools/list", "params": {...}}`
options.why: String IDs are allowed.

options.text: `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 0, "method": "tools/list", "params": {...}}`
options.why: Zero is a valid integer ID; only `null` is ruled out.

options.text: `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 42, "method": "server/discover", "params": {...}}`
options.why: A normal integer ID on a valid method; `params` carries the required `_meta`.

explanation: All MCP messages follow JSON-RPC 2.0, with stricter rules for IDs: requests must include a string or integer ID, the ID must not be `null`, and it must not match any other request the sender has issued that is still awaiting a response. The same envelope (method, params, id, then result or error) is used on every transport. (In the options, `{...}` stands for params that include the required `_meta`.)

stem: A client sends `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tasks/list", ...}` with valid `_meta` to a 2026-07-28 server over stdio. The server does not implement any method with that name. Which JSON-RPC error code should the error response carry? Type the number, including its sign.
explanation: `-32601` is the standard JSON-RPC "Method not found" code. MCP reuses the standard codes (`-32700` parse error, `-32600` invalid request, `-32601` method not found, `-32602` invalid params, `-32603` internal error) for general protocol failures. (`tasks/list` was removed when tasks moved into an extension, so a modern server is right to reject it.)

stem: Under revision 2026-07-28, a server that needs the user's confirmation in the middle of a `tools/call` may send its own JSON-RPC `elicitation/create` request to the client and wait for the client's response.

options.text: True
options.why: That was allowed up to 2025-11-25, but not any more.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. Servers must not initiate JSON-RPC requests; they return an `InputRequiredResult` and the client retries the original request with the answers.

explanation: In 2026-07-28 every interaction starts with the client: clients send requests and notifications, and servers send responses and request-scoped notifications. Servers **MUST NOT** initiate JSON-RPC requests, and clients do not send JSON-RPC responses. When a server needs input, it answers with `resultType: "input_required"` and the client retries with `inputResponses` (the Multi Round-Trip Requests pattern).

stem: In revision 2026-07-28, which `_meta` fields **must** appear on every client request? (Choose two.)

options.text: `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo`
options.why: Clients **SHOULD** include it on every request, but it is not required.

options.text: `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities`
options.why: Required on every request; an empty object means no optional capabilities.

options.text: `progressToken`
options.why: Optional; it only opts a request into progress notifications.

options.text: `io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel`
options.why: Optional; if absent, the server must not send log notifications for that request.

options.text: `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion`
options.why: Required on every request: it states the protocol version for that request.

explanation: Because there is no handshake, each request carries what the server needs: the protocol version and the client capabilities relevant to it. A request missing either is malformed and must be rejected with `-32602` (and HTTP 400). `clientInfo` is a SHOULD, and `progressToken` and `logLevel` are per-request opt-ins.

stem: MCP is often called "a USB-C port for AI applications". Where does that analogy fall short?

options.text: MCP also defines what the messages mean (primitives, capabilities, consent), not just the connector shape
options.why: A plug standard says little about meaning; MCP specifies the messages and their semantics too.

options.text: MCP cannot carry data in both directions
options.why: MCP is bidirectional: requests flow one way, responses and notifications the other.

options.text: MCP only connects one device at a time, while USB-C hubs connect many
options.why: An MCP host connects to many servers at once, one client per server.

options.text: USB-C is a proprietary connector owned by one vendor, while MCP is open, so the comparison misleads about licensing
options.why: USB-C is an industry standard, so this is not where the analogy breaks.

explanation: The official introduction uses USB-C to explain standardisation: build a server once and plug it into any host. But MCP is more than a connector. It defines primitives with distinct control models (model-controlled tools, application-driven resources, user-invoked prompts), capability negotiation, consent responsibilities for the host, and authorization for remote servers.

stem:
Your 2026-07-28 client receives this result from a server it reached through a dual-era fallback:

```json
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "result": {"tools": [{"name": "search", "inputSchema": {"type": "object"}}]}}
```

There is no `resultType`. How must the client treat it?

options.text: As a notification, because it lacks a type marker
options.why: It has an `id` and a `result`, so it is a response by JSON-RPC rules.

options.text: As `"input_required"`, and retry the request with empty `inputResponses`
options.why: Nothing indicates the server needs input; an interim result would carry `inputRequests` or `requestState`.

options.text: As `"complete"`, because servers on earlier revisions never send `resultType`
options.why: The spec requires clients to treat an absent `resultType` from earlier-protocol servers as complete.

options.text: As invalid, because every result must carry `resultType`
options.why: That rule binds servers implementing 2026-07-28; for older servers, clients must assume complete.

explanation: Every 2026-07-28 result must include `resultType`: `"complete"` for final results and `"input_required"` for Multi Round-Trip interim results. For backward compatibility, a client talking to a server on an earlier revision **MUST** treat an absent `resultType` as `"complete"`. This lets dual-era clients process legacy results unchanged.

stem: A modern server returns `"resultType": "deferred"` to a client that declared no extensions. Assume no core value or advertised extension defines `"deferred"`. What should the client do?

options.text: Treat it as invalid: unrecognised `resultType` values must be considered invalid
options.why: Unrecognised `resultType` values must be considered invalid, so the client should not guess at the shape.

options.text: Treat it as `"complete"` and read whatever fields are present
options.why: Only an *absent* `resultType` defaults to complete, and only for servers on earlier revisions.

options.text: Ignore it silently and wait for a later response with the same ID
options.why: A response is final for its ID; no second response will arrive.

options.text: Keep polling the server with the same request ID until the result type changes to complete
options.why: Request IDs must not be reused, and nothing in core defines polling for this value.

explanation: `resultType` is polymorphic: core defines `"complete"` and `"input_required"`, and extensions **MAY** add values, but only those advertised via capabilities belong in the supported set. A value the client does not recognise **MUST** be considered invalid. That stops a server from silently pushing extension behaviour onto a client that never opted in.

stem: Which of these server behaviours break the statelessness rules of revision 2026-07-28? (Choose two.)

options.text: Treating each stdio process as one conversation and storing a draft email in process memory between tool calls
options.why: A connection or process is not a session; clients may interleave unrelated requests on the same transport.

options.text: Remembering the capabilities declared on the first request over a stdio connection and applying them to later requests that omit elicitation
options.why: Servers must not rely on prior requests over the same connection for capabilities; each request declares its own.

options.text: Caching its own `tools/list` result and returning the same list to every client
options.why: List endpoints no longer vary per connection, so a shared, deterministic list is fine.

options.text: Reading the protocol version from each request's `_meta` before processing it
options.why: This is what statelessness requires.

options.text: Returning a server-minted `cart_id` from one tool and accepting it as an argument to later tools
options.why: This is the recommended pattern: state that spans requests is referenced by an explicit identifier the client passes each time.

explanation: In 2026-07-28 a server processes each request independently. It **MUST NOT** rely on prior requests over the same connection to establish capabilities, version or identity, and it should not treat a connection or stdio process as a conversation. State that spans requests **MUST** be referenced by an explicit identifier the client passes on each request.

stem: You are building a 2026-07-28 server with tools `start_order`, `add_item` and `checkout`. The cart must survive across calls, and the server runs on several stateless replicas. Which design follows the specification?

options.text: Mint an `Mcp-Session-Id` header on the first call and key the cart by it
options.why: Protocol-level sessions and `Mcp-Session-Id` were removed in 2026-07-28.

options.text: Key the cart by the TCP connection and turn on sticky load balancing so every call from that connection reaches the same replica
options.why: Servers should not require clients to reuse the same connection, and connection identity is not a session.

options.text: `start_order` returns a server-minted cart ID that later tools take as an argument, resolved from shared storage
options.why: Explicit, server-minted handles passed as arguments are how the spec says to carry cross-call state.

options.text: Key the cart by the `clientInfo` name and version from `_meta`
options.why: `clientInfo` is self-reported, optional and shared by every user of the same client software.

explanation: Revision 2026-07-28 removed protocol sessions. Servers that need cross-call state use explicit, server-minted handles passed as ordinary tool arguments. That keeps every request self-contained, so any replica can serve it if the handle resolves through shared storage. (How to protect handles from guessing is covered under security.)

stem: A 2026-07-28 HTTP server receives a `tools/call` for `delete_repo`. Its handler needs to ask the user to confirm through elicitation, but the request's `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` is `{}`. What should the server do?

options.text: Delete the repository without confirmation, since the client cannot ask
options.why: Silently skipping a safety step is unsafe, and the spec defines an explicit error for this case.

options.text: Return a successful result with `isError: true` and the text "confirmation unavailable" so the model can explain
options.why: This is a protocol-level capability failure with a defined error code, not a tool execution error.

options.text: Send the elicitation anyway, because most clients support it
options.why: A server **MUST NOT** rely on capabilities the client has not declared.

options.text: Return HTTP 400 with error `-32021` listing `elicitation` in `data.requiredCapabilities`
options.why: The spec requires this error, with the missing capabilities listed, and HTTP status 400.

explanation: Capabilities are declared on each request. If processing a request requires a capability the client did not include, the server **MUST** return `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` (`-32021`) with `data.requiredCapabilities`, and on HTTP the status **MUST** be 400. The client can then retry with the capability if it actually supports it, or tell the user.

stem: A 2026-07-28 client sends `tools/call` with `"name": "get_wether"` (a typo). The server has no tool with that name. Which JSON-RPC error code does the specification's own example use for an unknown tool? Type the number, including its sign.
explanation: An unknown tool name is an invalid parameter of the `tools/call` method, so the spec returns `-32602` (Invalid params), as in its example `"Unknown tool: invalid_tool_name"`. It is not `-32601`: the method `tools/call` exists. Revision 2026-07-28 also moved resource-not-found from `-32002` to `-32602` for the same reason.

stem: Match each failure with the JSON-RPC error code a 2026-07-28 server should return.

options.text: `-32601` Method not found
options.why: The method name is unknown to the server.

options.text: `-32021` Missing required client capability
options.why: Processing needs a capability the client did not declare.

options.text: `-32700` Parse error
options.why: The bytes are not valid JSON.

options.text: `-32602` Invalid params
options.why: The method exists but its params are wrong or incomplete.

prompts.text: The request body is truncated mid-object and cannot be parsed as JSON
The client calls `logging/setLevel`, which this revision removed
A tool needs elicitation but the request declared no elicitation capability

explanation: Malformed JSON is a parse error. Calling a method the server does not implement (`logging/setLevel` was removed in 2026-07-28) is method-not-found. A request missing a required `_meta` field is malformed and **MUST** be rejected with `-32602`. A capability the request needs but did not declare gets the MCP-specific `-32021`.

stem: Put the steps of the progress pattern in order for a long-running `tools/call`.

options.text: The server sends the final response to the request
The server sends `notifications/progress` messages whose `progress` value increases each time
The client sends the request with that token in `_meta.progressToken`
No further progress notifications are sent for that token
The client picks a progress token that is unique among its active requests

explanation: Progress is opt-in: the client puts a string or integer `progressToken` in the request's `_meta`, unique across active requests. The server **MAY** then send `notifications/progress` with the token, a `progress` value that **MUST** increase with each notification, and optional `total` and `message`. Progress notifications **MUST** stop after completion. A server may also choose to send none.

stem: A user clicks **Stop** while a long `tools/call` is running. Which description of cancellation in 2026-07-28 is correct?

options.text: HTTP: close that request's SSE stream. stdio: send `notifications/cancelled` with its ID
options.why: Each transport has its own signal, and the protocol rules are otherwise the same.

options.text: On both transports the client sends `notifications/cancelled`, and the server replies with a cancellation result
options.why: On HTTP, closing the stream is the signal, and servers should not send a response for a cancelled request.

options.text: On stdio the client kills and restarts the server process, because stdio has no per-request channel
options.why: Killing the process would abort every other in-flight request; stdio uses `notifications/cancelled` instead.

options.text: The client sends a `cancel` request and waits for an acknowledgment before freeing resources
options.why: Cancellation is a fire-and-forget notification; there is no acknowledgment.

explanation: On Streamable HTTP, each request has its own response stream, so closing it is an unambiguous cancellation signal and no `notifications/cancelled` is expected. On stdio, all traffic shares one channel, so the client **MUST** send `notifications/cancelled` referencing the request ID. Either way the server should stop work, free resources and not send a response.

stem: A stdio client sends `notifications/cancelled` for request 17 just as the server finishes it. Which statements about this race are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: The client must resend the cancellation until the server confirms it
options.why: There is no confirmation; cancellation is fire-and-forget.

options.text: The server must reply to the cancellation notification with an error so the client knows it was too late
options.why: Notifications never get responses; invalid or late cancellations are simply ignored.

options.text: The server may ignore the cancellation if processing has already completed
options.why: Servers **MAY** ignore cancellations for unknown or already-completed requests.

options.text: The server should roll back the completed work to honour the cancellation
options.why: Nothing requires rollback; the cancellation arrived too late to apply.

options.text: The client should ignore a response for request 17 that arrives after it cancelled
options.why: The client **SHOULD** ignore any response to the cancelled request that arrives afterward.

explanation: Because of latency, a cancellation can arrive after a request finished, or even after its response was sent. Both sides **MUST** handle this race gracefully: the server may ignore cancellations for unknown or completed requests, and the client should ignore late responses to requests it cancelled. Invalid cancellation notifications are ignored, keeping notifications fire-and-forget.

stem: Match each reserved `_meta` key with its purpose.

options.text: `io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId`
options.why: Correlates a notification with its subscription.

options.text: `traceparent`
options.why: W3C Trace Context for OpenTelemetry.

options.text: `io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel`
options.why: Per-request minimum log level.

options.text: `progressToken`
options.why: Opts a request into progress notifications.

prompts.text: The client wants `notifications/progress` updates for this one request
The client wants log messages at `warning` and above for this request only
A gateway propagates a distributed-tracing span context to the server
A notification on a listen stream must say which `subscriptions/listen` request it belongs to

explanation: `progressToken` opts into progress. `io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel` replaced the removed `logging/setLevel` RPC (logging itself is deprecated). `traceparent`, `tracestate` and `baggage` are reserved for OpenTelemetry and must follow W3C formats. `io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId` carries the JSON-RPC ID of the `subscriptions/listen` request on every notification delivered on that stream.

stem: A server may safely enable admin-only tools when a request's `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo` says the client is the company's internal admin console.

options.text: True
options.why: `clientInfo` is self-reported and unverified, so anyone can claim to be the admin console.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct. `clientInfo` and `serverInfo` are for display, logging and debugging, and **SHOULD NOT** be used for security decisions.

explanation: Both `clientInfo` and `serverInfo` are self-reported by the sender and are not verified by the protocol. Implementations **SHOULD NOT** use them to change behaviour and **SHOULD NOT** rely on them for security decisions. Gate privileged tools on authenticated identity (for example OAuth scopes on an HTTP server) instead.

stem: An architect proposes using MCP for a travel agent to delegate hotel booking to a separate booking agent owned by another team, which runs its own multi-step reasoning. Another engineer suggests the A2A (Agent2Agent) protocol. Which statement best captures the difference?

options.text: MCP only works for local tools on the same machine, so any collaboration with a remote team's agent has to use A2A instead
options.why: MCP supports remote servers over Streamable HTTP.

options.text: They are identical; the choice only affects JSON field names
options.why: Their models differ: MCP exposes primitives to a host, while A2A models tasks exchanged between peer agents.

options.text: A2A is the newer version of MCP, so MCP should no longer be used
options.why: They are separate protocols with different goals; MCP has its own active revisions.

options.text: MCP connects an agent to its tools and context; A2A lets agents delegate tasks to other agents. They complement each other
options.why: This is the usual split: MCP for agent-to-tool and context, A2A for agent-to-agent delegation.

explanation: MCP standardises how a host and its model reach tools, resources and prompts. A2A focuses on agents discovering each other and delegating tasks to peers that do their own reasoning. Real systems often use both: each agent uses MCP for its own tools, and A2A to hand work to other agents.

stem:
A client library sends this message to cancel a request over stdio:

```json
{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 99, "method": "notifications/cancelled", "params": {"requestId": 12}}
```

What is wrong with it?

options.text: It carries an `id`, which makes it a request rather than a notification; notifications must not include an ID
options.why: Notifications **MUST NOT** include an ID. With `id: 99` the receiver would treat it as a request expecting a response.

options.text: A `reason` field is required
options.why: `reason` is optional.

options.text: `requestId` must be a string, so `12` is invalid
options.why: Request IDs may be strings or integers; `12` is fine if request 12 was sent with an integer ID.

options.text: Cancellation on stdio must be done by closing stdin, not by a message
options.why: Closing stdin shuts down the whole server. On stdio, `notifications/cancelled` is the required mechanism.

explanation: The message type is determined by shape. A notification has `method` and optional `params` but **MUST NOT** include an `id`, and the receiver **MUST NOT** respond. Adding an `id` turns the message into a request with an unknown result shape. `notifications/cancelled` needs only `requestId` and an optional `reason`.

stem: Your team builds an MCP server and wants an application-specific error code for "upstream quota exhausted". Which choice follows the 2026-07-28 error-code allocation policy?

options.text: Use a code outside the JSON-RPC reserved range of -32768 to -32000, for example `-31001`
options.why: New codes for purposes the spec does not define **SHOULD** be allocated outside the reserved range.

options.text: Use `-32603` Internal error with the quota detail in `message`
options.why: That works but loses a distinct code. The question asks how to allocate a dedicated one.

options.text: Use `-32010`, because `-32000` to `-32019` is for implementation-defined errors
options.why: That legacy sub-range is closed to new allocations: new codes **MUST NOT** be allocated there.

options.text: Use `-32050`, since `-32020` to `-32099` is free for server errors
options.why: That sub-range is reserved for the MCP specification; implementations **MUST NOT** emit codes there that the spec does not define.

explanation: JSON-RPC reserves `-32768` to `-32000`. MCP splits its server-error range: `-32000` to `-32019` is legacy (no new allocations; receivers must not assume meanings, except `-32002`), and `-32020` to `-32099` is reserved for codes defined by the MCP spec, such as `-32020` HeaderMismatch, `-32021` MissingRequiredClientCapability and `-32022` UnsupportedProtocolVersion. Application errors go elsewhere in the integer space.

stem: Your MCP gateway already uses OpenTelemetry and wants traces to continue into backend MCP servers, over stdio as well as HTTP. Where should the trace context go?

options.text: In `_meta` under `io.modelcontextprotocol/traceparent`, because every reserved `_meta` key needs the MCP prefix
options.why: The OpenTelemetry keys are a deliberate exception to the prefix rule; they are bare `traceparent`, `tracestate` and `baggage`.

options.text: In `params._meta` as `traceparent` (plus optional `tracestate`, `baggage`) in W3C format
options.why: These keys are reserved for exactly this purpose and travel inside the message, so they work on every transport.

options.text: Only in an HTTP `traceparent` header, because stdio cannot carry trace context
options.why: `_meta` travels inside the JSON-RPC message, so stdio can carry it too.

options.text: Inside the tool's `arguments`, as a `trace_id` parameter
options.why: That pollutes the tool schema the model sees. The spec reserves `_meta` keys for trace propagation.

explanation: Revision 2026-07-28 documents OpenTelemetry trace context propagation in `_meta`: `traceparent`, `tracestate` and `baggage` are reserved, unprefixed keys whose values **MUST** follow W3C Trace Context and W3C Baggage. The exception exists for compatibility with existing implementations and the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for MCP.

stem: Your company owns `acme.dev` and is defining a custom MCP extension for audit trails, advertised in the `extensions` capability. Which identifier follows the rules?

options.text: `acme.dev/audit-trail`
options.why: Prefixes **SHOULD** use reverse DNS notation, so `acme.dev` should be written `dev.acme`.

options.text: `dev.mcp/audit-trail`
options.why: Any prefix whose second label is `mcp` or `modelcontextprotocol` is reserved for MCP itself.

options.text: `audit-trail`
options.why: Extension identifiers require a prefix; an unprefixed name is not allowed.

options.text: `dev.acme/audit-trail`
options.why: This is a reverse-DNS prefix you own, followed by `/` and a valid name.

explanation: Extension identifiers follow the `_meta` key naming rules with a **mandatory** prefix: dot-separated labels then `/`, preferably in reverse DNS form. Prefixes where the second label is `modelcontextprotocol` or `mcp` (for example `io.modelcontextprotocol/` or `dev.mcp/`) are reserved, while `com.example.mcp/` is not, because its second label is `example`. Official extensions use `io.modelcontextprotocol/`.

stem: Which situation is the best fit for a plain OpenAPI-described integration instead of building an MCP server?

options.text: The integration needs tools plus reusable prompt templates and readable resources
options.why: MCP has first-class primitives for all three, while OpenAPI only describes HTTP operations.

options.text: The tool list changes at runtime and hosts must learn about new tools without redeploying
options.why: MCP supports dynamic listing and list-changed notifications; a static OpenAPI file does not give hosts this.

options.text: Several AI hosts (IDE, chat app, internal agent) all need the same Jira and GitHub tools
options.why: Reuse across many hosts is exactly the N x M case MCP addresses.

options.text: One internal app with its own hard-coded agent calls one vendor API, and no other host will ever reuse the integration
options.why: With a single consumer and no cross-host reuse, MCP's interoperability benefit is small and direct integration is simpler.

explanation: MCP pays off when capabilities must be discoverable by many hosts, change at runtime, or use primitives beyond plain operations. If exactly one application talks to one API with a fixed set of calls, an OpenAPI spec or direct function definitions may be simpler. Senior interviewers want to hear the trade-off, not "MCP everywhere".

stem: Leadership mandates "expose every internal API as an MCP tool". Which are **weak** reasons to wrap a given API in MCP? (Choose two.)

options.text: The API has 300 fine-grained endpoints, and wrapping each one 1:1 means models must choose among 300 near-identical tools
options.why: Mirroring every endpoint floods the model's tool list; a few workflow-level tools work better.

options.text: Users want to use the capability from both their IDE and a chat assistant
options.why: Two different hosts consuming one server is the core MCP benefit.

options.text: Several assistants across the company need the same capability
options.why: Reuse across hosts is a strong reason to adopt MCP.

options.text: The capability's tool set changes as teams add features, and hosts should pick up changes at runtime
options.why: Runtime discovery is a real MCP advantage.

options.text: The API is called by one hard-coded backend job that will never be driven by an AI host
options.why: With no AI host consuming it, an MCP layer adds maintenance and attack surface for no benefit.

explanation: MCP is valuable where AI hosts need runtime-discoverable, reusable capabilities. It is a poor fit for integrations with no AI consumer, and blind 1:1 endpoint wrapping hurts model tool selection. A good answer pushes back on the mandate: wrap what AI hosts need, at workflow granularity, and leave plain service-to-service calls alone.

stem: In a debrief, you are asked which parts of running MCP in production are genuinely hard. Which two are the strongest answers? (Choose two.)

options.text: Authorization for remote servers: OAuth discovery, client registration and validating that tokens were issued for this server
options.why: Remote auth involves several RFCs and is a frequent source of real-world bugs.

options.text: Deciding how far to trust server-provided tool descriptions and results, which can carry prompt injection
options.why: Tool metadata and outputs are untrusted input to the model, so hosts need consent and isolation strategies.

options.text: Writing the `jsonrpc: "2.0"` field on every message
options.why: This is boilerplate that SDKs handle.

options.text: Serialising a `tools/list` response as JSON
options.why: Every SDK does this for you; it is not a real difficulty.

options.text: Choosing between integer and string JSON-RPC IDs
options.why: Both are allowed; this is a trivial choice.

explanation: Experienced practitioners point to auth and trust: OAuth 2.1 flows with protected resource metadata, audience-bound tokens and registration for remote servers; and the fact that tool descriptions and results flow into the model's context, so a malicious or compromised server can inject instructions. Envelope mechanics are handled by SDKs.

stem: Low-level design: your agent host must support tools from native code, from OpenAPI specs and from MCP servers, with one approval UI and no name clashes. Which design is strongest?

options.text: Give each source its own approval flow so teams can evolve them independently
options.why: Separate approval paths lead to inconsistent consent and audit gaps.

options.text: A unified registry with per-source adapters, namespaced tool names and one execution path for approval and logging
options.why: Adapters normalise sources, namespacing avoids collisions, and one execution path enforces policy consistently.

options.text: Merge all tools into one flat list keyed by bare tool name, letting later registrations overwrite earlier ones
options.why: Two servers can both expose `search`; silent overwrites cause wrong-tool execution.

options.text: Convert every OpenAPI and native tool into a separate MCP server process, then let the model call the servers directly
options.why: Models never call servers directly, and one process per tool adds overhead without solving naming or approval.

explanation: A host is the policy point: it aggregates tools from several MCP clients and other sources. A registry with per-source adapters exposes one normalised tool shape to the model, namespacing (for example by server) prevents collisions, and a single execution pipeline applies consent, timeouts, logging and result handling to every call regardless of origin.

stem: A stdio client calls a slow tool with a 30-second timeout that resets on progress, plus a 5-minute hard cap. Put the client's actions in the order they happen when the server keeps sending progress but never finishes.

options.text: Send the `tools/call` request with a `progressToken` in `_meta` and start both timers
Reset the 30-second timer each time a matching `notifications/progress` arrives
Ignore any response for that request ID that arrives later
Send `notifications/cancelled` with the request's ID and stop waiting
Reach the 5-minute hard cap, even though progress is still arriving

explanation: Implementations **SHOULD** set timeouts on every request and **MAY** reset the clock on progress notifications, but **SHOULD** always enforce a maximum timeout so a misbehaving peer cannot hold a request open forever. On timeout the sender cancels: on stdio by sending `notifications/cancelled`, on HTTP by closing the response stream. Late responses to cancelled requests are ignored.

stem: Under load, a custom client starts showing tool results from the wrong calls. Logs show it numbers requests with a counter that resets to 1 whenever a UI tab reloads, while older requests from that tab can still be in flight on the same stdio connection. What is the root cause?

options.text: The server must echo `_meta.progressToken` in responses and fails to
options.why: Responses are correlated by JSON-RPC `id`, not by progress token.

options.text: Integer IDs are not allowed; switching to strings fixes correlation
options.why: Integers are allowed. Uniqueness among in-flight requests is what matters.

options.text: Request IDs are reused while older requests with those IDs are still in flight
options.why: A request ID **MUST NOT** match the ID of any other request the sender issued that has not yet been answered.

options.text: stdio cannot carry concurrent requests, so the client must wait for each response before sending the next request
options.why: stdio can carry many in-flight requests; responses are correlated by ID.

explanation: On stdio all responses share one stdout stream and are matched to requests only by `id`. If two in-flight requests share an ID, the client cannot tell which response belongs to which. Use IDs that are unique per sender for as long as a request is outstanding, for example a connection-wide counter or UUIDs, not per-tab counters.

stem: A host sends two concurrent requests to the same server over one stdio connection. Request A (`tools/call` for `deploy`) declares `{"elicitation": {}}`. Request B (`tools/call` for `rollback`) declares `{}`. Both tools need user confirmation. What should the server do?

options.text: Elicit for A; reject B with `-32021`, since capabilities are judged per request
options.why: Servers **MUST NOT** infer capabilities from prior or parallel requests; B declared nothing.

options.text: Use elicitation for both, since the same client declared it on the same connection
options.why: Connection identity is not a session, and the spec forbids inferring capabilities from other requests.

options.text: Reject both, because capability declarations must match across a connection
options.why: Nothing requires consistency between requests; each is judged on its own `_meta`.

options.text: Queue B until A finishes, then reuse A's capabilities
options.why: That still infers capabilities from another request, which is exactly what is forbidden.

explanation: In 2026-07-28, client capabilities are declared per request (an empty object means no optional capabilities), and servers **MUST NOT** infer capabilities from prior requests. A host might legitimately allow elicitation in one context and not another, for example a background agent with no user present. The server rejects B with `MissingRequiredClientCapabilityError` listing `elicitation`.

stem: A buggy client writes a truncated message to a server's stdin: `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 5, "method": "tools/li`. What should the error response look like?

options.text: A `-32601` error, because `tools/li` is not a known method
options.why: Parsing fails before method dispatch, so this is a parse error, not method-not-found.

options.text: A `-32700` parse error, with the `id` member omitted because the ID could not be read from the malformed message
options.why: Error responses may omit the ID only when it could not be read, which is exactly the parse-error case.

options.text: No response at all, since malformed messages are treated as notifications
options.why: Only well-formed messages without an ID are notifications. A parse failure gets an error response.

options.text: A `-32700` parse error with `"id": 5`, because the server can see the ID in the raw text
options.why: The message cannot be parsed as JSON, so the server cannot reliably extract an ID.

explanation: Error responses **MUST** include the ID of the request they answer, except where the ID could not be read because the request was malformed. That is why `id` is optional on `JSONRPCErrorResponse`. Parse errors use the standard `-32700`. Diagnosing this tells you the client is breaking stdio framing, for example by splitting one message across writes or embedding newlines.

stem: A 2026-07-28 server streams `notifications/message` debug logs for every request, and a client complains about noise. The server calls `ctx.log()` freely. What does the spec say?

options.text: The client must call `logging/setLevel` once to lower the level for the whole connection
options.why: `logging/setLevel` was removed; the level is set per request in `_meta`.

options.text: Without `logLevel` in a request's `_meta`, the server must not send it log notifications; Logging is deprecated anyway
options.why: Log messages are opt-in per request, and Logging is deprecated in 2026-07-28.

options.text: Logs belong on the `subscriptions/listen` stream, so the client should simply not subscribe
options.why: Request-scoped notifications such as `notifications/message` flow on the originating request's stream, not the listen stream.

options.text: Servers may emit logs freely on every request, and it is the client's job to filter out whatever it does not want to display
options.why: Without `logLevel` in a request, the server **MUST NOT** send log notifications for it.

explanation: Revision 2026-07-28 removed `logging/setLevel`: a client opts into logs per request with `_meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/logLevel"]`, and servers **MUST NOT** emit `notifications/message` for requests without it. The Logging feature is also deprecated (earliest removal in the first revision released on or after 2027-07-28). The suggested migration is stderr for stdio servers and OpenTelemetry for observability.
